note: Fact base for the Cognition.X Simulation Studio: branching control-discipline scenarios driven by pack data. Every scenario is tied to a real track in data/blocks.csv and carries that track's witnessed transfer check verbatim, so the studio can never be mistaken for the check. Scenarios with a trades kind are localized by the host app to a real, publicly known site ({site}); the others take a place anchor from the host. Authored by the maintainers; reviewed like any pack.
law: Simulate what is dangerous, expensive or rare; practice live what is safe, cheap and common; debrief every run. Nothing energized, suspended or moving is practiced live in a classroom studio, and no simulation claims to certify. Simulation ≠ certification.
run_note: A simulation run is practice. It is not a witnessed check, it is not evidence of competence, and it is never a credential. Simulation ≠ certification.

difficulty.name: Rehearsal
difficulty.what: The five decision points, in order.

difficulty.name: Complications
difficulty.what: One complication injected at a seeded position.

difficulty.name: Full drill
difficulty.what: Both complications injected. Recommended only after a clean rehearsal.

next_rule: After a run: 85% or better moves the recommended difficulty up one level; under 50% moves it down; otherwise it stays. The recommendation is advice to the learner and the teacher, never a gate.

disciplines.name: Verify before you act
disciplines.what: Test it, measure it, read the tag, prove the meter. A reading is not a proof until the instrument is proved.

disciplines.name: Stop-work authority
disciplines.what: Anyone can halt the work. Halting is never punished. Rank does not change the edge.

disciplines.name: Say it out loud
disciplines.what: Announce, confirm back, hand over, write it down. The log is the last control of the day.

disciplines.name: The order is the safety
disciplines.what: Lock, then tag, then test. Alarm, then fight, then leave. Steps in order, none skipped.

disciplines.name: Escalate, do not improvise
disciplines.what: Call the person whose job it is. Not your ticket, not your sign-off.

disciplines.name: The person in front of you
disciplines.what: The crew, the public, the learner, the patient. Welfare is a control, not a courtesy.

scenarios.track: The simulation studio: the jobsite in the classroom
scenarios.title: The deck edge
scenarios.brief: You are on the crew at {site}. The morning task is laying metal deck on the third floor. The edge guardrail on the north side is down where a beam was landed yesterday, and the foreman is on the phone.
simulated: Working at height with a missing guardrail
A crane pick over the deck
Fall-arrest rescue
live: Tying off to a bench-mounted anchor
Reading a deck layout drawing
Inspecting a harness on the bench

steps.prompt: Your lead points at the north bay and says 'start there'. The guardrail is down. What first?

options.t: Tie off to the nearest anchor and start where the rail is still up, then flag the gap to the lead before anyone works the north bay.
options.c: The crew keeps working where it is protected. The gap goes on the board before anyone is near it.

options.t: Start on the north bay but stay a metre back from the edge.
options.c: There is no line, no rail and a metre of open deck. One misstep at height is the whole day.

options.t: Wait for the foreman to get off the phone before doing anything.
options.c: Safe, but the crew loses twenty minutes it did not need to lose. The protected bays were fine to start.

steps.prompt: The rail is still down and the lead says 'we're behind, just work it'. You are the newest person here.

options.t: Say it plainly: 'I'm not working an open edge without a rail or a line. Let's rig a line or get the rail up.' Stop-work is anyone's.
options.c: The lead grumbles and then nods. A perimeter cable goes up in fifteen minutes. Nobody says anything about it again.

options.t: Work it, but slowly and carefully.
options.c: Careful is not a control. The hazard has not changed; only your confidence has.

options.t: Ask the lead to show you how they want it done.
options.c: You have opened a conversation, but the edge is still open. Ask for the control, not the technique.

steps.prompt: A crane pick is coming over the deck. The signaller shouts 'load coming up'. Where do you stand?

options.t: Out from under the load path, in the signaller's sight, and say 'clear' back so they hear you.
options.c: You are seen and heard. The load passes with nobody under it.

options.t: Under the load, steadying it by hand so it lands square.
options.c: Nobody stands under a suspended load. Tag lines exist so hands do not.

options.t: Wherever you are — you keep working, the crane crew has it.
options.c: Probably fine. But 'probably' is not a place to stand when steel is in the air.

steps.prompt: A sheet of deck is bowed and does not sit on the beam flange. Two screws will pull it down.

options.t: Stop, check the beam and the sheet. A sheet that does not bear is a sheet that can drop when someone stands on it.
options.c: The beam is a hair out of line. The lead sees it and calls the ironworkers back. That is how it is supposed to go.

options.t: Pull it down with screws and move on.
options.c: You have hidden a bearing problem under fasteners. Someone will find it by stepping on it.

options.t: Leave the sheet loose and tell the lead at break.
options.c: Telling is right. An unfastened sheet on a deck for an hour is a trap for anyone walking it.

steps.prompt: End of shift. The rail is back up, the deck is half laid. What goes in the handover?

options.t: Where the deck is fastened, where it is loose, the bowed sheet and the beam, and that the north rail was down this morning.
options.c: The night crew walks onto a deck they can read. The handover is the last control of the day.

options.t: 'Half done, north side next.'
options.c: The loose sheet and the beam are now nobody's knowledge.

options.t: Tell the lead verbally and go home.
options.c: The lead knows; the board does not. Say it and write it.

complications.prompt: Wind picks up. The signaller says the crane will keep going, the pick is 'light'.

options.t: Ask the operator whether the site's wind limit for lifts has been checked, and hold the deck crew back until it has.
options.c: The operator checks the anemometer. It is under the limit; the lift goes ahead, with a number behind it.

options.t: Keep working — light picks are fine in wind.
options.c: A light sheet of deck in wind is a sail, not a light pick.

options.t: Stop everything and refuse to continue until the wind drops.
options.c: Stopping is always permitted. But the control here is a measured limit, not a feeling.

complications.prompt: A visiting engineer walks the deck without a harness to look at the beam.

options.t: Say it to them directly and courteously: on this deck everyone ties off, and hand them a spare harness.
options.c: They apologise and clip in. Rank does not change the edge.

options.t: Say nothing — they are the engineer.
options.c: The edge does not know who they are.

options.t: Tell the lead later that the engineer was not tied off.
options.c: After is too late for the walk they just did.

debrief: Where in this run did you have the authority to stop work, and did you use it?
Which control was a measured limit and which was a feeling?
What would the night crew have needed from you that you nearly did not give?

scenarios.track: Power back on: the grid after the wind
scenarios.title: Lockout at the substation
scenarios.role: Apprentice electrician on a restoration crew
scenarios.brief: You are at {site}. A feeder is out and the crew is replacing a damaged section. Your lead hands you the lockout kit and says the breaker is 'already open'.
simulated: Working on a feeder that may be energised
Backfeed from a customer generator
An arc-flash event
live: Applying a lock and tag to a training panel
Testing a meter on a known source
Reading a one-line diagram

steps.prompt: The breaker is 'already open'. What happens before anyone touches the conductor?

options.t: Your own lock and tag on the isolation point, then test for dead with a meter you have just proved on a live source.
options.c: Lock, tag, test-before-touch. The order is the safety, and it is yours, not the lead's word.

options.t: Trust the lead — they opened it — and start work.
options.c: A breaker described as open is a rumour until your meter says so.

options.t: Test for dead with your meter, then start.
options.c: Testing is right. Without your lock, someone else can close the breaker while your hands are on it.

steps.prompt: Your meter reads dead. You prove the meter on a live source afterwards and it does not light.

options.t: Treat the conductor as live. The meter is faulty — the 'dead' reading proves nothing. Get another meter and prove it live-dead-live.
options.c: The second meter proves live on the source and dead on the feeder. Now you know.

options.t: The first reading was dead, so it is dead.
options.c: A meter that cannot see a live source cannot be trusted to have seen a dead one.

options.t: Tell the lead the meter is odd and wait.
options.c: Right to say it. The control is a proved meter; ask for one.

steps.prompt: A house on the block has a portable generator humming. The feeder is locked out upstream.

options.t: Say it out loud to the crew and the lead: possible backfeed. Test the section again and get the customer's transfer switch checked before work continues.
options.c: The generator is on a proper transfer switch. Five minutes to know it, against a lifetime not to.

options.t: Generators are on the customer side — not your problem.
options.c: A generator without a transfer switch backfeeds the line you are about to hold.

options.t: Unplug the customer's generator yourself.
options.c: You do not touch a customer's equipment. Report it and get it checked.

steps.prompt: The lead wants to remove your lock to test the repair 'for a second'.

options.t: Only the person who put a lock on removes it, and only when they are clear. You remove your own lock after you and your tools are off the line.
options.c: Everyone clears, every lock comes off in order, the test is run. Nobody was on the line.

options.t: Give the lead your key.
options.c: A key handed over is a lock that no longer protects anyone.

options.t: Refuse and walk away.
options.c: Refusing is right. Walking away without clearing the line and saying so leaves the crew guessing.

steps.prompt: Repair done. Re-energising. What is the last check?

options.t: Head count against the lock log, all locks off, all crew clear and told, then the breaker closes on a spoken count.
options.c: Everyone hears the count. The feeder comes back with nobody near it.

options.t: Close the breaker — the work is finished.
options.c: Finished for you. The count is what tells you it is finished for everyone.

options.t: Ask the lead if everyone is clear.
options.c: Ask the log, then ask the people. 'Is everyone clear' is a question the lock log answers first.

complications.prompt: A customer walks up angry: they have had no power for two days and want to know why you are 'standing around'.

options.t: Someone steps away from the work to speak with them plainly — what is being done and roughly when — while the crew keeps its attention on the line.
options.c: They calm down when they are told the truth. The crew never took its eyes off the work.

options.t: Ignore them and work faster.
options.c: Faster is where the mistakes live, and the person is still angry.

options.t: Stop the whole job to talk to them.
options.c: Kind, but the whole crew does not need to stop for one conversation.

complications.prompt: It starts to rain on the open cabinet.

options.t: Cover the cabinet, pause the work on the exposed section, and say so.
options.c: A tarp and a pause. The work restarts dry.

options.t: Keep going — it is locked out.
options.c: Locked out from the feeder, not from the rain in a cabinet you will re-energise.

options.t: Close the cabinet and leave the section for tomorrow without telling anyone.
options.c: Safe today, a mystery tomorrow. Write it down.

debrief: Whose lock protects you? Say the rule in your own words.
What did the faulty meter teach you about the difference between a reading and a proof?
Which conversation in this run was a control, not a courtesy?

transfer.check: From the ground and eyes only, sketch the path power takes from the nearest pole to your meter, naming each piece.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: no live work on energized or potentially energized conductors — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.333 'qualified person' rules and the host's policy; minors observe and practise on de-energized training panels only. Louisiana and most states also require an employment certificate for minors.

scenarios.track: Water in, water out: pumps, canals and the storm
scenarios.title: The pump station in the rain
scenarios.brief: You are at {site} on a night when the rain gauge has climbed for three hours. One of four pumps is tagged out for a bearing. The canal is rising and the lead operator has gone to check the intake screens.
simulated: Starting a pump against a rising canal
A screen blockage with someone on the deck
Loss of station power
live: Reading a level gauge and a pump curve
Walking the station's start-up checklist on a mock panel
Radio protocol on the bench

steps.prompt: The canal level is a hand-width below the start point for the second pump. The screens are being cleared.

options.t: Radio the lead: level, trend, what you intend to do next, and confirm the screen deck is clear before any pump starts.
options.c: 'Deck clear, start two when it hits the mark.' Now two people know one plan.

options.t: Start the second pump now — better early than late.
options.c: Someone is on the screen deck. A pump starting pulls water and whatever is on the deck toward it.

options.t: Wait for the lead to come back and decide.
options.c: The lead has a radio. Use it; the water does not wait for footsteps.

steps.prompt: The level reaches the mark. The lead confirms the deck is clear. The second pump starts and its amps read high.

options.t: Watch it for the first minute against the curve: high amps at start is normal, high amps that stay is a blockage or a bearing.
options.c: Amps settle in forty seconds. You logged the number and the time.

options.t: Stop it immediately — high amps means damage.
options.c: Stopping is always permitted, and against a rising canal it has a cost. Know what the curve says first.

options.t: Ignore the amps — the pump is running.
options.c: Amps are the pump talking. A bearing that seizes under load takes the motor with it.

steps.prompt: The tagged-out pump would help. Its tag says 'bearing — do not run'. The level keeps climbing.

options.t: The tag stands. Escalate to the duty engineer for the third pump's start and for the flood-stage plan.
options.c: The engineer authorises the third pump and calls the upstream station. The tagged pump stays tagged.

options.t: Run the tagged pump for a short while — the storm justifies it.
options.c: A tag is someone's judgement that running it breaks it. Breaking it in the storm leaves three pumps forever.

options.t: Start the third pump yourself without a call.
options.c: Right pump, wrong path. The call takes a minute and puts the decision where it belongs.

steps.prompt: Station lights flicker. Standby generator should pick up.

options.t: Confirm the transfer happened — generator running, pumps still turning, alarms acknowledged — and tell the lead and the engineer.
options.c: The generator took the load. You checked rather than assumed.

options.t: Assume it worked — the lights came back.
options.c: Lights on a separate circuit tell you about lights.

options.t: Go outside to look at the generator.
options.c: Looking is good. The panel tells you first and keeps you at the controls.

steps.prompt: The rain slows. Level falling. What goes in the log before shift ends?

options.t: Times, levels, every start and stop, the tagged pump untouched, the generator transfer and the calls made.
options.c: The day shift reads a night that makes sense. The tag and the transfer are on record.

options.t: 'Storm handled, all good.'
options.c: The numbers are gone. The next storm learns nothing.

options.t: Log the pump starts only.
options.c: Half the story. The transfer and the escalation are the parts the engineer needs.

complications.prompt: A neighbour appears at the gate with a phone, filming, shouting that their street is flooding.

options.t: Send one person to tell them what the station is doing and where to report the street, and keep the controls staffed.
options.c: They leave with a number to call. The pumps never lost an operator.

options.t: Let them in to see for themselves.
options.c: A pump station in a storm is no place for the public.

options.t: Ignore them.
options.c: Understandable, and their street is real. A minute of truth costs nothing.

complications.prompt: The radio goes silent — the lead is not answering.

options.t: Try once more, then use the phone or the station alarm. Someone on the deck who is not answering is the first priority.
options.c: Their radio battery died. You found that out by going to look, with someone on the controls.

options.t: Carry on — they will call back.
options.c: A silent radio in a storm is a missing person until proven otherwise.

options.t: Leave the controls to go find them.
options.c: Right instinct, wrong order. Get the controls covered first.

debrief: What did the tag protect, and who did it protect from?
Which numbers did you log, and which decision would have been impossible without them?
When was a radio call a control rather than a report?

transfer.check: On a real elevation map, find your own ground height relative to the river and the lake, and state where your rain goes.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: FLSA HO 7 (hoisting) and HO 17 (excavation) apply at a pump station's sumps and pits; confined-space entry (29 CFR 1910.146) is never a youth task. Control-room observation and dry runs on a mock panel are the youth-appropriate forms.

scenarios.track: The port and the crane: cargo across the levee
scenarios.title: The container that is not square
scenarios.role: Lasher and signaller-in-training on a wharf crew
scenarios.brief: You are on the wharf at {site}. A ship-to-shore crane is discharging. One container comes off with a twistlock that has not released on one corner, and the box hangs a few degrees off level.
simulated: A suspended container hanging off level
A person in the crane's slew path
A dropped load
live: Hand signals on the bench
Reading a bay plan
Inspecting a twistlock in the hand

steps.prompt: The box is off level, ten metres up. The crane operator cannot see the corner.

options.t: Give the stop signal, then radio: 'stop — corner not released — hold'. Nobody moves under it.
options.c: The load holds. The operator knew exactly why.

options.t: Wave the operator to keep going slowly.
options.c: A hung twistlock lets go when it wants to. Slow does not change the physics.

options.t: Shout to the crew to move back and let the operator work it out.
options.c: Moving back is right. The operator cannot see what you see; say it.

steps.prompt: The operator asks: 'can someone go up and knock it?'

options.t: No one goes near a suspended load. Land it on the wharf or in the cell, then release the corner with the box on the ground.
options.c: The box lands in an empty cell. The twistlock is freed with two feet on steel.

options.t: You go — you are the closest.
options.c: Nobody stands under or beside a hung load. That is the first rule of the wharf and the last.

options.t: Suggest the operator jog it to free the lock.
options.c: Sometimes done, never safe. The ground is the control.

steps.prompt: A truck driver walks toward the crane's path to ask when his box is coming.

options.t: Get his attention, stop him with a signal and a word, walk him back to the marked lane, and tell the operator there was a person in the path.
options.c: He is embarrassed and safe. The operator adds it to the day's log.

options.t: Let him — he works here.
options.c: Working here is not the same as being seen by the crane.

options.t: Shout from where you are.
options.c: He may not hear you over the crane. Signal and go.

steps.prompt: A twistlock on the next box looks worn — the head is rounded.

options.t: Take it out of service, tag it, tell the lead, and swap in a checked one before the box lifts.
options.c: One twistlock in a bin, tagged. One box lifted square.

options.t: It is probably fine — they all look like that.
options.c: 'They all look like that' is how a fleet of worn parts stays in service.

options.t: Use it and mention it later.
options.c: Later is after the lift. Say it before.

steps.prompt: Shift change. What does the next crew hear?

options.t: The hung box, the person in the path, the tagged twistlock and its bin, and where the crane stopped.
options.c: The next crew walks on knowing what today learned.

options.t: 'Normal shift.'
options.c: Three near-events, no record.

options.t: Tell the lead about the twistlock only.
options.c: The person in the path is the one they most need to hear.

complications.prompt: A squall rolls in and the crane's wind alarm sounds mid-lift.

options.t: Land the load if it is safe to do so, or hold and clear the area, on the operator's call — and clear everyone from under the boom.
options.c: The box is set down. The crane is stowed until the alarm clears.

options.t: Finish the row quickly before it gets worse.
options.c: A wind alarm is a limit, not advice.

options.t: Stop and run for cover.
options.c: Getting clear is right. The load in the air needs a plan first, and the operator has it.

complications.prompt: The lead tells you to skip the walk-around on the spreader to catch up.

options.t: Say no and do the walk-around; offer to make time elsewhere.
options.c: Forty seconds. The spreader was fine, and you knew it was.

options.t: Skip it — the lead said so.
options.c: The lead's instruction does not inspect a spreader.

options.t: Do a quick look instead of the checklist.
options.c: A look is better than nothing and worse than the list.

debrief: Which stop did you call and how did the operator know why?
What is the difference between a worn part and a part that is out of service?
Who was the person you protected who did not know they needed it?

transfer.check: Find, on a real map, the port facility nearest your parish and name two things that actually move through it.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: FLSA HO 7 bars minors from operating or assisting on cranes, hoists and forklifts, with no student-learner exemption; lashing under a suspended load is an adult task. The hand-signal and bay-plan practices are the youth forms.

scenarios.track: Roads shared: safety for every user
scenarios.title: The yard crossing
scenarios.role: Trainee on a rail-yard maintenance crew
scenarios.brief: You are at {site}. Your crew needs to cross two live tracks to reach a switch that needs a heater checked. Movements in the yard are controlled by the tower, and a train is due.
simulated: Crossing live track
A movement that starts without warning
Working foul of a track
live: Reading a yard diagram
Radio protocol on the bench
Walking a marked crossing in the studio

steps.prompt: The switch is fifty metres away across two tracks. The lead is on the radio to the tower.

options.t: Wait for the tower's protection — track and time — to be confirmed and repeated back before anyone steps foul.
options.c: 'Track two and three, fifteen minutes, protection in place.' Now you cross.

options.t: Cross now while it is quiet.
options.c: Quiet is not protection. Yard movements do not announce themselves.

options.t: Cross one track at a time, looking both ways.
options.c: Looking is a habit, not a control. The tower's protection is the control.

steps.prompt: Protection is confirmed for fifteen minutes. You are at the switch after four. The heater check takes eight.

options.t: Set a hard stop at twelve minutes to be clear of the tracks, and say it to the crew.
options.c: The check finishes in seven. You are clear with five minutes in hand, and everyone knew the number.

options.t: Work until the job is done — the tower will call.
options.c: The tower protects the time you asked for. Overrun is on you.

options.t: Ask the tower for more time now, just in case.
options.c: Reasonable, but the time you have is enough if you manage it. Ask when you need it, with the real number.

steps.prompt: A colleague steps onto track one — outside the protection — to get a tool from the truck.

options.t: Call it: 'stop — track one is not protected'. Get them back the way they came.
options.c: They freeze, turn, and come back. Nobody argues with a call like that.

options.t: It is only a step — let them go.
options.c: Track one is live. A step is enough.

options.t: Tell them afterwards that they should not have.
options.c: After is a lecture; during is a control.

steps.prompt: The heater element is warm but the switch points are icing. The fix is a different crew's job.

options.t: Record what you found, report it to the lead and the tower, and clear the track on time.
options.c: The signal crew is called. Your time expires with you standing clear.

options.t: Try to fix the points yourself.
options.c: Not your qualification, not your time window.

options.t: Leave it; someone will notice.
options.c: They will — when a train notices for them. Report it.

steps.prompt: Clear of the track at eleven minutes. What do you tell the tower?

options.t: 'Crew clear of tracks two and three, protection released, points icing on switch nine reported to the lead.'
options.c: The tower releases the tracks and logs the switch. Two crews now know.

options.t: Nothing — the time ran out anyway.
options.c: Protection is released by a voice, not a clock.

options.t: 'We're done.'
options.c: Done where? Which tracks? The tower needs the words.

complications.prompt: Your radio chirps low battery in the middle of the protected window.

options.t: Tell the lead now, use the lead's radio for the release, and note the battery in the log.
options.c: The release goes through on the lead's radio. Yours is on charge by the afternoon.

options.t: It will last — carry on.
options.c: A radio that dies during protection is a crew the tower cannot reach.

options.t: Go back to the truck for a spare.
options.c: That is a crossing you did not plan. Use the lead's radio.

complications.prompt: Fog rolls in and you cannot see the far end of the yard.

options.t: Say it to the tower; ask whether the protection changes with visibility and whether movements are restricted.
options.c: The tower slows movements to restricted speed and confirms your protection stands.

options.t: Fog does not matter under protection.
options.c: Your protection stands, but you can no longer see anything that breaches it.

options.t: Leave the tracks at once.
options.c: Never wrong. But you had protection; a call would have let you finish.

debrief: What does 'protection' mean here, and who grants it?
Where did you set a number ahead of time, and why did that matter?
Which stop was the hardest to call, and why?

transfer.check: Assess three real crossing points near a school or home, rank their risk with reasons, and demonstrate the safest use of the worst one.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: no minor works foul of a live track; rail-yard roles are adult roles under the carrier's rules. Youth practise the radio protocol, the yard diagram and the marked crossing in the studio only.

scenarios.title: The stage load-in
scenarios.role: Stagehand on a rigging and audio crew
scenarios.brief: You are at {site}. The truss is going up with lights and line-array boxes on it. The stage manager wants doors open in three hours, and a truck is late.
simulated: A truss lift with a load imbalance
A motor with a slipping chain
Someone under a moving truss
live: Tying a bowline and a clove hitch at the bench
Reading a rigging plot
Setting up a console on the bench

steps.prompt: The head rigger calls 'going up' on the main truss. You are attaching the last cable.

options.t: Shout 'hold — hands on', finish and step out, then 'clear' before it moves.
options.c: The rigger holds, you clear, the truss goes up with nobody on it.

options.t: Finish quickly while it starts to move.
options.c: A truss that moves while you are on it takes your hands with it.

options.t: Let go and step back without saying anything.
options.c: Safe, but the rigger did not know you were there. Say it.

steps.prompt: The truss stops a metre off the deck. The plot says four motors; you count four, but one chain is slack.

options.t: Call it to the head rigger before it goes higher — a slack chain means one motor is not taking its share.
options.c: A motor had stalled. Fixed on the deck instead of at trim height.

options.t: It will tighten as it climbs.
options.c: A slack chain at a metre is a dropped corner at eight.

options.t: Pull the chain tight by hand.
options.c: Not your job, and the truss is live on the motors. Say it instead.

steps.prompt: The audio crew wants to fly the line arrays before the truss is trimmed and locked, to save time.

options.t: Sequence stands: truss trimmed, motors locked, checked, then the arrays. Say it kindly and hold it.
options.c: Twenty minutes later the arrays fly on a truss that will not move. Nobody remembers the argument.

options.t: Let them — the schedule is real.
options.c: The schedule is real, and so is a truss that shifts under the array's weight.

options.t: Ask the stage manager to decide.
options.c: The rigging order is the head rigger's call, not the stage manager's. Escalate to the right person.

steps.prompt: A runner walks under the truss with a coffee tray while it is trimming.

options.t: Stop them with a word and a hand, walk them out, and remind the crew: nobody under a moving truss.
options.c: They laugh and walk round. The rigger says 'thank you' without looking down.

options.t: It is only a runner — they are quick.
options.c: Quick is not a control.

options.t: Shout from the deck.
options.c: Shouting can startle the wrong person. Go and stop them.

steps.prompt: Doors in forty minutes. The plot has a lighting fixture the truck never delivered. The designer wants it 'anything that works' from the case.

options.t: Fly what is rated for the position and note the substitution; a fixture at the wrong weight or clamp waits for the right one.
options.c: A lighter fixture on a rated clamp goes up. The note is on the plot for tomorrow.

options.t: Put whatever fits up there — it is one fixture.
options.c: One fixture with the wrong clamp over an audience is the whole show.

options.t: Refuse to hang anything not on the plot.
options.c: Refusing is allowed. A rated substitute was the reasonable answer.

complications.prompt: A thunderstorm is forecast to pass over at doors. The stage roof is up.

options.t: Ask the stage manager for the weather plan and the wind-speed limit for the roof, and who calls the hold.
options.c: There is a plan, a number and a name. That is what you needed.

options.t: Storms are the promoter's problem.
options.c: The roof is the crew's problem and the audience's.

options.t: Start taking down the arrays now to be safe.
options.c: Not your call; ask for the plan.

complications.prompt: The head rigger gets a phone call and walks off mid-lift with the truss at head height.

options.t: Call 'hold' so the motors stop, keep everyone clear, and wait for the rigger to come back to the controller.
options.c: The truss holds at head height with nobody under it. The rigger is back in a minute.

options.t: Take over the controller.
options.c: One person runs the lift. You are not that person today.

options.t: Keep working around it.
options.c: Working under a truss with nobody on the controls is not working around it.

debrief: What is the order of operations for a lift, and what did skipping it risk?
Which call was yours to make and which belonged to the head rigger?
What went on the plot for tomorrow, and why does that matter?

transfer.check: Build and play a forty-five-minute set list with written reasoning for its order, then revise it after one performance.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: FLSA HO 7 covers motorised hoists and truss lifts; working at height and under a moving truss is an adult task. Knots, plot reading and console setup at the bench are the youth forms.

scenarios.title: The school boiler room
scenarios.role: Facilities apprentice on a school campus
scenarios.brief: You are at {site}, an occupied school on a cold morning. A teacher reports a classroom radiator is cold and a smell 'like gas' near the boiler room. The head custodian is across campus.
simulated: A suspected gas leak in an occupied building
Working in a boiler room with a fault
An evacuation decision
live: Bleeding a radiator on a training rig
Using a gas detector on a known test source
Reading a boiler's sequence of operation

steps.prompt: 'Like gas' near the boiler room. Children in the corridor. What first?

options.t: Do not enter, do not touch switches. Get people away from the door, call the head custodian and the office, and start the gas procedure.
options.c: The corridor clears. The office knows. The procedure is running before anyone opens a door.

options.t: Go in and check the boiler quickly.
options.c: A room that might hold gas is not a room you check quickly.

options.t: Open the boiler room door and windows to air it out.
options.c: Ventilation helps, but opening a door into gas with a light switch beside it is the wrong order. Call first.

steps.prompt: The office asks: 'is it an evacuation?'

options.t: Say what you know and do not know: a smell reported, not confirmed, boiler room isolated, detector on its way; recommend moving the nearest classes now while the head custodian decides.
options.c: Two classes move to the hall. The head custodian arrives with the detector.

options.t: 'No, it is probably nothing.'
options.c: Probably is not what the office asked for.

options.t: 'Yes, evacuate everyone.'
options.c: Never wrong to be careful. But the decision belongs to the person with the detector and the procedure; give them the facts.

steps.prompt: Detector reads clean. The smell was a dead animal in the duct. The cold radiator is real.

options.t: Log the false alarm as a real drill, then diagnose the radiator: is it air, a closed valve, or the zone? Questions and checks before tools.
options.c: A closed zone valve on the floor above. Nobody replaced a radiator that was never broken.

options.t: Replace the radiator — it is cold.
options.c: Cold is a symptom. You have not found the fault.

options.t: Bleed the radiator and see.
options.c: A reasonable first check, but do the questions first — the valve would have told you.

steps.prompt: The zone valve is stuck. Freeing it needs the boiler off for twenty minutes during lessons.

options.t: Tell the office which rooms lose heat, for how long, and when; then do it at the agreed time.
options.c: Two rooms warm up an hour later than they wanted, and everyone knew why.

options.t: Do it now — twenty minutes is nothing.
options.c: Twenty minutes in a cold room full of children is something to the teacher in it.

options.t: Leave it until the holidays.
options.c: A cold classroom for six weeks is a decision, not a postponement.

steps.prompt: End of day. What does the head custodian find in the log?

options.t: The smell report, who was moved and when, the detector reading, the duct, the stuck valve and the heat outage window.
options.c: A day that can be audited. The false alarm becomes the drill the school never had.

options.t: 'Radiator fixed.'
options.c: The evacuation decision is gone from the record.

options.t: A note about the valve only.
options.c: The valve is the least of what happened today.

complications.prompt: A teacher insists on going back into the classroom nearest the boiler room for a bag.

options.t: Say no, kindly and clearly: nobody goes past the line until the detector says so; offer to get the bag afterwards.
options.c: They wait. Four minutes later the detector clears and they get the bag.

options.t: Let them — it is thirty seconds.
options.c: The line is the line.

options.t: Go and get the bag yourself.
options.c: Kind, and the same rule applies to you.

complications.prompt: The boiler room's detector battery is flat when the head custodian arrives.

options.t: Treat the room as unverified: keep it closed, call for a working detector or the gas utility, and say so to the office.
options.c: The utility arrives with a detector in fifteen minutes. The room was closed the whole time.

options.t: Go in and sniff carefully.
options.c: Your nose is not calibrated and it is attached to you.

options.t: Open the door and wait ten minutes before going in.
options.c: Better than sniffing, still a guess. A detector is the control.

debrief: What did you refuse to do, and what did that refusal protect?
Where did 'questions and checks before tools' save a replacement?
What did the office need from you that was neither 'yes' nor 'no'?

transfer.check: Diagnose one real fault to a most-likely cause using questions and checks alone, before any tool touches it.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: gas-suspected areas, boiler rooms and rooftop plant are excluded from youth work under the host's facilities policy; the diagnostic questions and a training rig are the youth forms.

scenarios.title: The lathe with the missing guard
scenarios.role: First-year machinist in a fabrication shop
scenarios.brief: You are on the floor at {site}. Your job today is turning a shaft on a lathe whose chuck guard was removed last week 'for a big job' and not put back. The shop is loud and the supervisor is at the far end.
simulated: Running a lathe without its guard
Entanglement
A chuck key left in the chuck
live: Measuring with a micrometer at the bench
Reading a drawing and planning cuts
Guard inspection on a powered-down machine

steps.prompt: The guard is off. The job is waiting. What first?

options.t: Do not start it. Find the guard or a supervisor; a machine without its guard is out of service until it has one.
options.c: The guard is in a cabinet. Five minutes to fit it. The job starts guarded.

options.t: Run it carefully — you know what you are doing.
options.c: Careful is not a guard. Entanglement takes a tenth of a second.

options.t: Run a different machine and leave the lathe alone.
options.c: Safe for you, not for whoever is next. Tell someone.

steps.prompt: Guard on. Before the spindle turns, what is the sequence?

options.t: Chuck key out and in your hand, work secured, guard closed, speed set for the material, hands clear, then start.
options.c: The key is in your pocket. The spindle turns with nothing in it that should not be.

options.t: Start it and adjust as it runs.
options.c: A chuck key left in a chuck becomes a projectile at the first turn.

options.t: Ask a colleague to check your setup.
options.c: Good habit. The sequence is still yours to run first.

steps.prompt: The cut chatters and swarf comes off in long blue ribbons.

options.t: Stop the feed, then the spindle; adjust speed and feed; clear the swarf with a hook, never a hand, with the spindle stopped.
options.c: The next cut is quiet and the swarf breaks short.

options.t: Pull the swarf clear while it runs.
options.c: Swarf is a hot, sharp ribbon wrapped around a spinning part. Hands stay out.

options.t: Keep going — chatter is normal.
options.c: Chatter is the machine telling you the numbers are wrong. Listen.

steps.prompt: The supervisor comes by and says the guard 'slows the big jobs' and asks you to leave it off after yours.

options.t: Say that you will leave the machine guarded and tag it if the guard has to come off, so the next person knows. Offer to raise it at the toolbox talk.
options.c: The supervisor shrugs and agrees to the tag. The guard stays.

options.t: Do as asked.
options.c: An instruction to remove a guard is an instruction you do not follow.

options.t: Say nothing and leave it on anyway.
options.c: Right outcome, silent. The next person still does not know the story.

steps.prompt: Shaft finished. What does the next operator find?

options.t: A clean, guarded machine, the key on its hook, the log noting the guard's return and the supervisor's request.
options.c: The shop's record now says the guard belongs on. That is a control for everyone.

options.t: The machine as you left it mid-clean.
options.c: Swarf on the ways and a key somewhere.

options.t: Clean machine, nothing written.
options.c: Good for the machine. The story of the guard is lost.

complications.prompt: Your sleeve is loose and the shop is cold.

options.t: Roll the sleeve or change the jacket before the spindle turns. Loose cloth does not go near a lathe.
options.c: Cold wrists. Attached wrists.

options.t: Keep the sleeve — you will stay back.
options.c: Nobody stays back from a lathe.

options.t: Tuck the sleeve into a glove.
options.c: Gloves near a lathe are their own entanglement hazard. Roll it.

complications.prompt: A colleague's part jams on the machine next to you and they reach in while it runs.

options.t: Hit their emergency stop if you can reach it safely, or shout 'stop' — then talk.
options.c: The spindle stops. They pull their hand back. The talk happens after.

options.t: Mind your own machine.
options.c: On a shop floor, every machine is your business.

options.t: Tell them afterwards it was dangerous.
options.c: Afterwards is if there is an afterwards.

debrief: What makes a machine 'out of service', and who can declare it so?
Recite the start-up sequence. Which step protects against which hazard?
How did you disagree with a supervisor without making an enemy?

transfer.check: Interview somebody whose work was automated and write their account.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: FLSA HO 8 (metal-forming, punching, shearing) and HO 14 (power-driven saws, guillotine shears) apply in a machine shop; a lathe is not listed by HO but the host's youth policy and state child-labor law govern it, and a student-learner exemption needs a written agreement. Measuring, drawing and guard inspection on a powered-down machine are the youth forms.

scenarios.title: The small fire
scenarios.role: Fire warden in training on a site
scenarios.brief: You are the floor warden under {site}. A bin fire starts in a kitchenette on your floor. Twenty people are at their desks; one uses a wheelchair; the lift is not for fire use.
simulated: A fire that may outgrow an extinguisher
Smoke in a corridor
A stairwell evacuation with a wheelchair user
live: Extinguisher types matched to fuels on the bench
Walking the escape route
The roll-call sheet

steps.prompt: Smoke from the kitchenette. A bin is burning; flames are below waist height.

options.t: Raise the alarm first, then — with the exit at your back and the right extinguisher — attempt it once. If it is not out in seconds, leave.
options.c: Alarm sounding, extinguisher on the bin, out in four seconds. The exit was behind you the whole time.

options.t: Fight it first, alarm second.
options.c: If it grows while you fight it, nobody upstairs knows.

options.t: Leave it and evacuate.
options.c: Never wrong. A waist-high bin fire with the right extinguisher was the one fire you were trained to try.

steps.prompt: The alarm is sounding. People are gathering their bags.

options.t: Loud, plain, repeated: 'Leave now, no bags, stairs to the left, assembly point in the car park.' Sweep the floor as you go.
options.c: The floor is empty in ninety seconds. Two bags left behind. Correct.

options.t: Let them get their things — it is only a bin.
options.c: 'Only a bin' is what every fire was, once.

options.t: Go to the assembly point and count from there.
options.c: The count matters. The sweep is what makes the count true.

steps.prompt: Your colleague who uses a wheelchair is at the stairwell door. The evacuation chair is on the landing.

options.t: Stay with them, get them to the refuge at the landing, use the evac chair with the trained buddy, and tell the fire service via the warden radio where you are.
options.c: Refuge, radio, chair, ground floor. Nobody was left to wait alone.

options.t: Tell them to wait by the lift.
options.c: The lift is out. Waiting alone by it is the worst place on the floor.

options.t: Carry them down yourself.
options.c: Brave and dangerous for both of you. The chair and the buddy exist for this.

steps.prompt: At the assembly point, the count is one short: someone was in the toilet.

options.t: Report the missing person's name and last known location to the fire service or the chief warden. Nobody goes back in.
options.c: The fire service finds them on the stairs, fine. Your report sent them to the right place.

options.t: Go back in to look.
options.c: Wardens do not re-enter. That is what the report is for.

options.t: Assume they left another way.
options.c: They may have. Report it anyway; the fire service decides what to assume.

steps.prompt: All clear. What happens before people go back in?

options.t: The fire service or chief warden gives the all-clear, the bin and the kitchenette are checked, and the drill log records times, the count, the chair use and the bags.
options.c: The log is the next drill's lesson plan.

options.t: Send everyone back — it was small.
options.c: The all-clear is not yours to give.

options.t: Go back in yourself to check first.
options.c: The fire service checks; you report.

complications.prompt: The extinguisher you grab is water, and the bin has a laptop charger burning in it.

options.t: Stop. Do not use water on electrical fire. Get the CO2 or leave it and go.
options.c: CO2 from the next cabinet. Out in seconds, and nobody got a shock.

options.t: Use it anyway — water is water.
options.c: Water on a live electrical fire conducts.

options.t: Try to unplug the charger first.
options.c: You are reaching into a fire. Pick the right extinguisher instead.

complications.prompt: The stairwell is smoky at the second landing.

options.t: Turn back to the refuge, close the door, radio your position and use the alternate stair if it is clear.
options.c: The alternate stair is clean. The radio call means the fire service knew where you were.

options.t: Push through — it is only two floors.
options.c: Two floors of smoke is how people are found on stairs.

options.t: Wait on the landing for it to clear.
options.c: Waiting is better than pushing. A refuge and a call are better still.

debrief: Alarm, fight, leave: say the order and what each step depends on.
What did you do for the person who could not use the stairs, and what did you not do?
Where was the line you did not cross, and who did that protect?

transfer.check: Audit a real dwelling against the top ignition causes and eliminate or mitigate every finding, with photos.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.youth: Under 18: extinguisher and evacuation drills are appropriate at every age; interior firefighting is an adult, trained role. Junior programs run under the department's own rules.

scenarios.title: Entering the robot cell
scenarios.brief: A six-axis arm in a fenced cell has dropped a part. The line is stopped and the supervisor wants it cleared 'before the next cycle'. The cell has an interlocked gate, a light curtain and a teach pendant.
simulated: Entering a cell with a robot that may move
A restart while someone is inside
A pendant in the wrong mode
live: Tracing a stop circuit on a powered-down trainer
Reading a cell's safety drawing
Pendant mode selection with the drives off

steps.prompt: The part is on the floor inside the fence. The arm is still.

options.t: Stop the cell on the controller, open the interlocked gate so the safety circuit drops the drives, and take the key or your lock with you into the cell.
options.c: Drives off, key in your pocket, arm cannot move. The part takes ten seconds.

options.t: Reach through the light curtain — it is only a metre in.
options.c: A light curtain stops the cell when broken. Reaching around it does not.

options.t: Wait for the maintenance team.
options.c: Safe. Maintenance would have done exactly what the interlock lets you do. Know your cell.

steps.prompt: Still inside, you see the gripper is misaligned. Fixing it needs the arm jogged a few degrees.

options.t: Leave the cell, close the gate, and only then use the pendant in a reduced-speed manual mode with the enabling switch held; jog from outside if the cell allows, or with a second person watching the stop.
options.c: The arm jogs at reduced speed with your hand on the enabling switch and a colleague on the stop.

options.t: Jog it from inside — you are right there.
options.c: A jog from inside the envelope is a jog toward yourself.

options.t: Ask the supervisor to jog it while you hold the gripper.
options.c: Two people, one of them inside the envelope with the arm live. No.

steps.prompt: The supervisor asks you to bypass the gate interlock 'just for this shift' to save time on clears.

options.t: No. A bypassed interlock is a cell with no safety. Offer to time the clears and propose a faster safe procedure.
options.c: The supervisor accepts the timing study. The interlock stays.

options.t: Do it — they are the supervisor.
options.c: A supervisor's authority does not extend to removing a safety function.

options.t: Bypass it but tell everyone.
options.c: Telling people the cell is unsafe does not make it safe.

steps.prompt: Before restart, the light curtain shows a fault.

options.t: Do not restart. A faulted safety device is a stopped cell until it is fixed and tested by someone qualified.
options.c: Maintenance finds a misaligned emitter. Aligned, tested, logged, restarted.

options.t: Restart — the gate interlock is enough.
options.c: Each safety device covers a path the others do not. A faulted one is a gap.

options.t: Restart at reduced speed.
options.c: Reduced speed does not fix a device that cannot see you.

steps.prompt: End of shift. What is in the cell log?

options.t: The dropped part, the entry with drives off, the gripper jog with enabling switch, the refused bypass and the curtain fault with its fix.
options.c: The next operator reads a cell with a history.

options.t: 'Cleared a part.'
options.c: The refused bypass and the curtain fault vanish from memory.

options.t: The curtain fault only.
options.c: The bypass request is the one the safety lead needs to see.

complications.prompt: A visitor group arrives to watch the cell while you are inside.

options.t: Ask their guide to keep them outside the marked area and away from the controller until you are out and the gate is closed.
options.c: They watch from the line. You leave, the gate closes, the tour continues.

options.t: Ignore them.
options.c: A curious visitor at a controller is a hand on a button.

options.t: Come out immediately to greet them.
options.c: Finish the clear safely first, then greet.

complications.prompt: The pendant's enabling switch feels sticky and sometimes stays 'on'.

options.t: Tag the pendant out and report it. A sticky enabling switch is a dead-man that is not dead.
options.c: A replacement pendant by the afternoon. The sticky one is in the safety lead's hands.

options.t: Use it — you can work around it.
options.c: The enabling switch is the last protection when everything else is wrong.

options.t: Clean it and carry on.
options.c: Cleaning is fine after it has been tagged and tested.

debrief: What did the interlock do for you, and what did you do that it could not?
Which request did you refuse, and how did you leave the relationship intact?
Name each safety device in this cell and the path it protects.

transfer.check: Trace the stop circuit on a real cell and identify every trigger.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.title: First run of a new machine
scenarios.role: Commissioning trainee on a conveyor and sorter line
scenarios.brief: A new sorting line has been installed. The vendor's engineer has left. The plant manager wants the first live run this afternoon. The emergency-stop test has not been signed off.
simulated: A first run with an unproven stop circuit
A jam clearing on a running line
A mode mismatch between two controllers
live: Walking a commissioning checklist
Testing a stop button on a powered-down panel
Reading an I/O list

steps.prompt: The plant manager says 'run it, we will test the stops later'.

options.t: Stops are tested first, every one, with the line dry, and signed. Show the manager the checklist and the empty line in the signature box.
options.c: Forty minutes of stop tests. One button did nothing. That is why it is first.

options.t: Run it — the vendor said it was fine.
options.c: The vendor's word is not in the signature box.

options.t: Run it at slow speed with people watching.
options.c: Slow does not test a stop button that does nothing.

steps.prompt: Stop tests: one emergency-stop button on the far end does not stop the sorter.

options.t: Tag the line out of service, record the failure with its button number, and call the vendor and the plant electrician. No run until it is fixed and retested.
options.c: A wiring fault at the terminal. Fixed, retested, signed.

options.t: Note it and run anyway — the other stops work.
options.c: The person standing at the far end has the one stop that does nothing.

options.t: Fix the wiring yourself.
options.c: Not your ticket, not your sign-off. Call the electrician.

steps.prompt: Dry run. A guard door on the sorter opens and the sorter keeps running.

options.t: Stop it. An interlocked door that does not stop the machine is a failed safety function; record it and it joins the gap list.
options.c: Two gap items now. Both are why a dry run exists.

options.t: It is a dry run; nothing is in it.
options.c: The dry run found the fault. Ignoring the finding wastes the run.

options.t: Close the door and continue.
options.c: Closing the door does not fix the interlock.

steps.prompt: The manager wants a partial handover: run the conveyor only, sorter locked out, to ship today.

options.t: If the conveyor's stops and guards passed, a documented partial handover with the sorter physically locked out and the gap list attached is legitimate.
options.c: The conveyor runs. The sorter carries a lock. The gap list is on the door.

options.t: Refuse any run until everything passes.
options.c: Allowed. But the conveyor passed; a documented partial run was the honest middle.

options.t: Run both — the sorter faults were minor.
options.c: A failed stop and a failed interlock are not minor.

steps.prompt: What does the commissioning record say at the end of the day?

options.t: Every stop tested with results, the failed button and interlock with their fixes or open status, the partial handover with its lockout, and who signed.
options.c: The plant can read exactly what is safe to run.

options.t: 'Commissioned.'
options.c: The gap list is the record. Without it, the sorter is 'commissioned' with a door that does not stop it.

options.t: The failures only.
options.c: The passes matter too — they say what is safe to run tonight.

complications.prompt: The vendor's engineer answers the phone and offers to 'talk you through' a bypass of the door interlock so the line can ship.

options.t: Decline. A remote bypass on an unproven line is not a fix; ask for a site visit or a written change with retest.
options.c: The engineer comes on site next morning. The interlock is fixed properly.

options.t: Follow the instructions.
options.c: A bypass by phone is a bypass with nobody responsible.

options.t: Do it and note it in the log.
options.c: The log now records that you removed a safety function on purpose.

complications.prompt: A jam on the conveyor during the partial run.

options.t: Stop, lock out, clear the jam, restart on a count. Jams are cleared with the line dead.
options.c: Two minutes with the line dead. Restarted on a spoken count.

options.t: Clear it while it runs.
options.c: A running conveyor and a hand in a jam.

options.t: Wait for the electrician.
options.c: Clearing a jam with a lockout is within your competence. Use it.

debrief: What is a gap list and why did it save the day?
Which two safety functions failed, and how were they found?
When was a partial handover honest, and what made it so?

transfer.check: List the gap items for one real system.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.track: First aid: the first ten minutes
scenarios.title: The collapse in the corridor
scenarios.role: Lay first responder in a workplace or school
scenarios.brief: A colleague collapses in a corridor. They are not moving. A crowd forms. Someone shouts to 'do something'.
simulated: A casualty who may not be breathing
A crowd around a casualty
A defibrillator retrieval
live: CPR on a manikin
Recovery position with a partner
Locating the defibrillator on a map

steps.prompt: They are on the floor and not moving. What first?

options.t: Check the scene is safe, then the person: shout and shake, look for breathing. Send a named person to call emergency services and another for the defibrillator.
options.c: 'You — call. You — the AED by reception.' Two people now have jobs. Nobody is guessing.

options.t: Start chest compressions immediately.
options.c: If they are breathing, compressions are wrong; if the scene is unsafe, you are the next casualty.

options.t: Shout for someone to call for help.
options.c: 'Someone' is nobody. Point at a person and give them the task.

steps.prompt: Not breathing normally — occasional gasps.

options.t: Gasping is not breathing. Start compressions now, hard and fast in the centre of the chest, and keep going until the AED arrives.
options.c: Compressions started within a minute. The AED is on its way.

options.t: Wait — gasps mean they are breathing.
options.c: Agonal gasps are a sign of cardiac arrest, not of breathing.

options.t: Put them in the recovery position.
options.c: Recovery position is for someone breathing. This person is not.

steps.prompt: The AED arrives. The crowd is close.

options.t: Turn it on and follow its voice; have someone move the crowd back; attach pads to bare skin; everyone clear when it says so.
options.c: The AED analyses, advises a shock, everyone is clear, shock delivered.

options.t: Keep doing compressions and ignore the AED until help comes.
options.c: The AED is the thing most likely to restart a heart. Use it as soon as it arrives.

options.t: Wait for someone trained to use it.
options.c: The AED talks you through it. You are the trained person now.

steps.prompt: After the shock the person starts breathing and moaning.

options.t: Stop compressions, recovery position if breathing continues, keep the pads on, stay with them, and update the caller.
options.c: Breathing, on their side, pads on, ambulance three minutes out.

options.t: Take the pads off — they are fine now.
options.c: A heart that stopped once can stop again. The pads stay until paramedics say.

options.t: Sit them up and give water.
options.c: Kind, wrong. No food or drink; keep them lying down.

steps.prompt: Paramedics arrive. What do you tell them?

options.t: When they collapsed, what you saw, when compressions started, the AED's advice and shocks, when breathing returned, and anything the crowd knows about them.
options.c: The handover takes thirty seconds and is the most useful thing the paramedics hear all day.

options.t: 'They collapsed, we did CPR.'
options.c: The times are the story.

options.t: Let the crowd tell it.
options.c: You were the hands. Tell it yourself, in order.

complications.prompt: A bystander says they are a nurse and takes over compressions; their rhythm is much slower than yours.

options.t: Keep the AED running its prompts, say the rate out loud, and offer to swap every two minutes so nobody tires.
options.c: The rate comes up. Two minutes later you swap. The nurse thanks you.

options.t: Step back — they are a nurse.
options.c: A nurse is welcome. A slow rate is still a slow rate.

options.t: Push them aside.
options.c: Not needed. Say the rate; they will hear it.

complications.prompt: Someone starts filming.

options.t: Ask them to stop and to help by holding a door for the paramedics instead.
options.c: They pocket the phone and hold the door.

options.t: Ignore it — the casualty is the priority.
options.c: True. Someone else could have asked. The casualty's dignity is also care.

options.t: Stop compressions to confront them.
options.c: Nothing interrupts compressions except the AED and the paramedics.

debrief: Who did you name for what job, and why does naming matter?
What did 'gasping' mean, and what would you have done if you had guessed wrong?
What did you tell the paramedics, in what order?

transfer.check: Approach three staged casualty scenes, verbalising the hazard check and the decision to proceed, stage, or wait for each.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.track: The storm and the long memory
scenarios.title: Seventy-two hours out
scenarios.role: Family or hall lead in hurricane season
scenarios.brief: A storm is forecast to reach {site} in about seventy-two hours. The cone is wide. You are responsible for a household of four, including a grandparent on oxygen, and for the hall's records.
simulated: An evacuation decision under uncertainty
Loss of power to medical equipment
A road that closes
live: Building a go-bag on the bench
Reading the parish's evacuation zone map
Backing up records to a portable drive

steps.prompt: Seventy-two hours. The cone is wide. What now?

options.t: Check the parish's zone and the order status, fuel the car, fill prescriptions and the oxygen supplier's plan, back up the hall's ledger to a drive, and set a decision time for tomorrow.
options.c: A list, a tank of fuel, a backup drive, and a time. Uncertainty handled by sequence.

options.t: Wait for the cone to narrow before doing anything.
options.c: The cone narrows when it is too late to move slowly.

options.t: Leave now.
options.c: Early is never wrong for a household with medical needs. But leaving before the plan exists costs you the plan.

steps.prompt: Forty-eight hours. The oxygen supplier says deliveries stop tomorrow. No order for your zone yet.

options.t: The medical need decides, not the zone: move the grandparent to the arranged place inland tomorrow morning, with the supplier's out-of-area contact, whether or not an order comes.
options.c: They travel in daylight on open roads with a full tank of oxygen and a contact number.

options.t: Wait for the mandatory order.
options.c: Orders come for geography. Oxygen runs out for a person.

options.t: Buy a generator today.
options.c: Useful, and it does not replace supply. Move the person.

steps.prompt: Thirty-six hours. A neighbour says the highway is 'a parking lot' and they are staying.

options.t: Check the contraflow status and the parish's own channels rather than the neighbour's report; decide on the information, and share what you found with them.
options.c: Contraflow opened at six. The neighbour changes their mind when they see the source.

options.t: Stay — if the road is jammed there is no point.
options.c: A rumour is not a road report.

options.t: Leave immediately by back roads.
options.c: Back roads flood first. Check before you commit.

steps.prompt: Twenty-four hours. You are inland. The hall's building has the paper records and the sign-in sheets.

options.t: The drive backup is done. Nobody goes back for paper. Tell the hall's contact list where the backup is and who holds it.
options.c: Two people know where the records are. The paper is paper.

options.t: Drive back for the paper records.
options.c: Nothing on paper is worth a drive into a storm.

options.t: Say nothing — the drive is safe with you.
options.c: Safe and secret is half a backup. Tell someone.

steps.prompt: After the storm. Power out at the hall for a week. What do you write down?

options.t: The timeline: what you decided when, what information you used, what worked, what you would move earlier next time, and the grandparent's plan for next season.
options.c: The next storm inherits a plan with dates on it.

options.t: Nothing — it is over.
options.c: The long memory is written or it is lost.

options.t: A note that everyone was fine.
options.c: Fine is the outcome. The decisions are the lesson.

complications.prompt: The grandparent refuses to leave: they 'rode out the last one'.

options.t: Sit down with them, listen, then be plain about the oxygen supply and the delivery stop, and ask them to come for the family's sake. Involve the doctor if it helps.
options.c: The doctor's call settles it. They pack.

options.t: Leave them — it is their choice.
options.c: A person on oxygen without deliveries has not made a free choice; they have made an uninformed one.

options.t: Insist and argue.
options.c: Insisting rarely moves anyone. Facts and a doctor do.

complications.prompt: Your phone has no signal at the inland stop.

options.t: Use a landline, a neighbour's carrier, or a text (texts get through when calls do not) to tell the contact list where you are.
options.c: A text goes through. Two people know.

options.t: Wait for signal.
options.c: Waiting is a plan for signal, not for people.

options.t: Drive to find signal.
options.c: Try the landline first; the roads are the risk.

debrief: What decided the move: the zone, the order, or the person? Say why.
Which report did you check against a source, and what did you find?
What is written down now that was not written down before?

transfer.check: Build a documented timeline of the major storms that struck your own region, with each storm's principal lesson stated.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.track: Knife, fire and mise en place
scenarios.title: Friday service, the fryer
scenarios.brief: It is {site}. Tickets are eight deep. A fryer's oil is smoking, the chef is plating, and the dish pit is behind. A new runner has just walked through the line.
simulated: A grease fire
A burn at the fryer
A cross-contamination event under pressure
live: Knife cuts to size on real vegetables
Probe-thermometer readings
Extinguisher and fire-blanket drill on a cold station

steps.prompt: The fryer is smoking. What first?

options.t: Turn the fryer down or off, say 'fryer's smoking' loud enough for the chef, and keep water and wet cloths away from it.
options.c: The chef hears it. The oil settles. Nobody threw water.

options.t: Drop the next basket — it is only smoke.
options.c: Smoking oil is oil near its flash point. The next basket is the fire.

options.t: Pour a little cold oil in to cool it.
options.c: It might help; it might overflow. Turn it down and say it.

steps.prompt: A flame licks up from the fryer.

options.t: Lid or fire blanket over it, gas off, do not move it, do not use water. Call it: 'fire at the fryer'. Extinguisher only if it escapes the pan.
options.c: Blanket on, gas off, out in seconds. The line kept plating.

options.t: Throw water on it.
options.c: Water in burning oil is a fireball.

options.t: Carry the fryer basket outside.
options.c: Moving burning oil spreads it. Cover it where it is.

steps.prompt: Back in service. A runner reaches over the raw-chicken board to grab plated food.

options.t: Stop them, take the plate a different way, and re-run the board: wipe, sanitise, fresh board, fresh gloves.
options.c: A minute lost. A hundred covers protected.

options.t: Let it go — nothing touched.
options.c: 'Nothing touched' is not something you can see.

options.t: Shout at the runner.
options.c: Say it firmly and once; then fix the board. The runner is new.

steps.prompt: The ticket printer jams and the chef is shouting. You have a burn from the fryer's edge.

options.t: Cool the burn under running water for ten minutes, cover it, tell the chef you are off the fryer, and let the chef re-sequence the line.
options.c: Ten minutes of water. A dressing. The chef moves you to garnish.

options.t: Wrap it in a towel and keep going.
options.c: A burn keeps burning under a towel.

options.t: Put butter on it.
options.c: An old story. Water, not butter.

steps.prompt: Service ends. What is in the close-down?

options.t: Fryer cooled and cleaned, the near-fire noted for the chef, the burn in the accident book, the board incident and the runner's briefing.
options.c: The book shows a Friday that taught something.

options.t: Wipe down and go home.
options.c: The fire and the burn are gone from the record.

options.t: Tell the chef about the burn.
options.c: Say it and write it. The book is the memory.

complications.prompt: A customer with a nut allergy has a ticket in, and the garnish station has been pesto all night.

options.t: Call the allergy loud, clean the station or plate from a clean area with fresh tools, and confirm the plate by name before it leaves.
options.c: A clean plate, called twice. The customer never knew how close it was.

options.t: Wipe the board and carry on.
options.c: Wiping moves allergen around.

options.t: Refuse the ticket.
options.c: Sometimes right. A clean plate from a clean area was possible tonight.

complications.prompt: The dish pit sends back a knife in the sink under suds.

options.t: Say it to the pit and the chef: knives never go under water. Retrieve it by sight, with the water drained.
options.c: Drained sink, knife found by the handle. The pit learns the rule.

options.t: Fish for it.
options.c: A blade under suds finds hands.

options.t: Leave it for later.
options.c: Later is somebody else's hand.

debrief: What did you do to the fryer before you did anything to the fire?
Which stop was about a customer you could not see?
What would the accident book say about tonight, and why does that matter for the next new cook?

transfer.check: Produce a small dice, a julienne and a chiffonade to size on real vegetables, safely, in under ten minutes.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.track: Sourcing, safety and the supply line
scenarios.title: The delivery that is warm
scenarios.role: Receiving cook and food-safety lead in training
scenarios.brief: A delivery arrives at {site} on a hot afternoon. The driver is in a hurry. The chicken boxes feel cool but not cold, and the probe reads seven degrees. The freezer's alarm went off overnight.
simulated: Accepting a cold-chain failure
A freezer that thawed and refroze
Service on compromised stock
live: Probe readings on the bench
Reading a delivery log
Labelling and dating stock

steps.prompt: Seven degrees on the chicken. The driver wants a signature.

options.t: Reject the chicken, record the reading and time on the delivery note, and take a photo. Sign for what passed only.
options.c: The chicken goes back. The note says why, with a number.

options.t: Sign — seven is nearly five.
options.c: Nearly is the difference between a limit and a wish.

options.t: Accept it and cook it straight away.
options.c: Cooking kills bacteria, not toxins already made. Reject it.

steps.prompt: The freezer alarm log shows minus four for six hours overnight, now back at minus eighteen.

options.t: Treat the freezer contents as suspect: check for thaw signs, ice crystals and refreezing, discard anything that thawed, and report the alarm to the manager and the engineer.
options.c: Half a shelf discarded. The compressor is serviced that week.

options.t: It is frozen now, so it is fine.
options.c: Frozen now tells you about now.

options.t: Discard everything.
options.c: Safe, wasteful. Minus four for six hours is a check, not an automatic loss.

steps.prompt: The chef says the special tonight is the fish that was in that freezer.

options.t: Say it plainly: the fish thawed and refroze; it is out. Offer the alternative from stock that stayed cold.
options.c: A different special. Nobody eats a story.

options.t: Serve it — the chef decided.
options.c: The chef's menu does not change the freezer's log.

options.t: Serve it and mention the log later.
options.c: Later is after the plates.

steps.prompt: A new prep cook has put raw chicken on the top shelf of the walk-in above the salad.

options.t: Move it to the bottom shelf now, then show the cook the shelf order and why.
options.c: Salad below chicken becomes chicken below salad, and a cook who knows why.

options.t: Leave it — it is wrapped.
options.c: Wrap leaks. Gravity does not.

options.t: Tell the chef about the cook.
options.c: Fix the shelf first. Then teach.

steps.prompt: End of day. The records?

options.t: The rejected delivery with reading and photo, the freezer alarm and what was discarded, the special change, and the walk-in correction.
options.c: An inspector reads a kitchen that catches its own mistakes.

options.t: Nothing — no one got sick.
options.c: No one got sick because of what you did. Write it.

options.t: The rejected delivery only.
options.c: The freezer is the bigger story.

complications.prompt: The supplier calls and offers a credit if you 'just take the chicken this once'.

options.t: Decline. A credit does not change the temperature. Ask for a re-delivery in a refrigerated van.
options.c: A cold delivery arrives the next morning.

options.t: Accept the credit.
options.c: You have been paid to serve a risk.

options.t: Accept and cook it well done.
options.c: Well done is not a control for toxins.

complications.prompt: The probe thermometer's calibration check in ice water reads three degrees.

options.t: The probe is off by three. Recalibrate or replace it, and re-read anything measured today with a checked probe.
options.c: The chicken re-reads at ten with a good probe. Rejection stands, and then some.

options.t: Subtract three from everything.
options.c: Better than nothing; a checked probe is the control.

options.t: Ignore it — it is close.
options.c: Close is how a warm delivery reads cold.

debrief: What number turned a feeling into a decision?
Which discard was necessary and which would have been waste?
How did you say no to the chef and the supplier and keep both?

transfer.check: Log the temperatures of five foods through a full service with a probe thermometer and act correctly on one that fails.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.track: The parish: government closest to the door
scenarios.title: The drainage vote
scenarios.role: Resident and first-time public speaker at a parish council meeting
scenarios.brief: The council is voting tonight on a drainage project that would raise a fee and fix the street that floods outside your school. You have three minutes at public comment. A neighbour is angry and wants you to 'say something'.
simulated: Public comment under time and pressure
A heated exchange with a council member
A procedural motion that changes the vote
live: Reading an agenda and a fiscal note
Timing a three-minute statement
Finding the parish's public-records request form

steps.prompt: You have three minutes. What is the shape of the comment?

options.t: Name yourself and your street, state the fact (how many times it flooded, from the parish's own log), what you ask the council to do, and thank them. Under three minutes, written down.
options.c: Two minutes forty. The clerk enters it in the record.

options.t: Speak from the heart, as long as it takes.
options.c: The gavel comes at three minutes, mid-sentence.

options.t: Read the neighbour's list of grievances.
options.c: Their anger is real; the record needs your fact and your ask.

steps.prompt: A council member interrupts: 'where did you get that flooding number?'

options.t: Say the source: the parish drainage log, the dates, and offer to give the clerk the copy. Then continue.
options.c: 'Noted.' You continue with a minute to spare.

options.t: 'Everyone knows it floods.'
options.c: Everyone is not a source.

options.t: Argue with the council member.
options.c: An argument costs your time and your ask. The source was the answer.

steps.prompt: Another speaker says the fee will hurt fixed-income households.

options.t: Acknowledge it in your ask: fix the street and ask the council about a hardship deferral, which the fiscal note mentions. Both can be true.
options.c: The council member who interrupted you moves to add the deferral language.

options.t: Ignore it — it is not your point.
options.c: It is your neighbours' point, and the vote's.

options.t: Say the fee is worth it regardless.
options.c: Honest, and it leaves the fixed-income households without a friend in the room.

steps.prompt: A member moves to table the vote for a study.

options.t: Ask the chair, through the process, whether the study has a date and a scope; a study with a date is progress, a study without one is a shelf.
options.c: The chair asks the member. A ninety-day scope goes into the motion.

options.t: Shout from the floor.
