options.c: You are out of order and out of the record.

options.t: Leave in disgust.
options.c: Understandable. The date question was the useful one.

steps.prompt: After the meeting. What do you do with what happened?

options.t: Write to the clerk for the minutes and the motion text, tell the neighbours what was decided and when the study reports, and put the report date on the calendar.
options.c: Ninety days later you are back with the study in hand.

options.t: Nothing — they tabled it.
options.c: Tabled with a date is a next meeting, not an ending.

options.t: Post an angry summary online.
options.c: Fine to be angry. The minutes are the thing to share.

complications.prompt: The neighbour grabs the microphone after you and starts shouting at the council.

options.t: Let the chair handle the room; afterwards, offer to help the neighbour put their points in writing for the record.
options.c: They calm down outside. Their letter is on the next agenda.

options.t: Take the microphone back from them.
options.c: Not yours to take.

options.t: Leave them to it.
options.c: You could have helped afterwards. The letter matters.

complications.prompt: You are told the fiscal note is not on the website and the clerk's office is closed.

options.t: File a public-records request the next morning; ask the clerk at the meeting whether copies are available at the desk.
options.c: A copy is at the desk. The request is filed anyway, for the record.

options.t: Speak without it.
options.c: Your ask depends on what the fee actually is.

options.t: Use a number from a social post.
options.c: A post is a rumour with a screenshot.

debrief: What was your fact, your source and your ask? Say them in one breath.
What did you do when interrupted, and what would have cost you the room?
What is on your calendar now that was not before?

transfer.check: Produce the one-page profile of your own parish — population, seat, governing form, and three services it actually runs — from official sources.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.title: The fall at home
scenarios.role: Family carer for an older parent
scenarios.brief: Your parent, who lives alone and takes a blood thinner, has fallen in the kitchen. They are awake, embarrassed, and want to get up 'before anyone sees'. Their head hit the cabinet.
simulated: Moving someone after a fall
A head injury on a blood thinner
Refusing help you know is needed
live: Safe assisted standing with a partner
Reading a medication list
Finding the falls service number

steps.prompt: They want to get up now.

options.t: Ask them to stay put for a minute. Check: pain, where, can they move everything, are they bleeding, did they black out. The head, the blood thinner and the cabinet decide what happens next.
options.c: Sore hip, bump on the head, no blackout that they remember. Now you know what you are dealing with.

options.t: Help them up — they know their body.
options.c: Standing on a broken hip does more damage. Check first.

options.t: Call an ambulance immediately.
options.c: Not wrong. Thirty seconds of questions tells you whether it is the right call.

steps.prompt: Head bump, blood thinner, no obvious injury elsewhere.

options.t: A head knock on a blood thinner is a medical call every time, even if they feel fine. Ring the advice line or emergency services and say those words.
options.c: The nurse on the line says: bring them in. A scan shows a small bleed, caught early.

options.t: Watch them overnight.
options.c: A bleed on a blood thinner does not wait for morning.

options.t: Give them paracetamol and a cup of tea.
options.c: Kind. Not a control for a bleed. Make the call.

steps.prompt: They refuse: 'I am not going to the hospital for a bump.'

options.t: Listen, then be plain about the blood thinner and why this bump is different; offer to go with them and to call the doctor together. Respect the choice; make sure it is informed.
options.c: They go, grumbling, because you went too.

options.t: Insist and threaten to call anyway.
options.c: Threats end conversations.

options.t: Accept the refusal and leave it.
options.c: Their choice is theirs. It was not yet an informed one.

steps.prompt: At the hospital, the nurse asks about the medication and the falls history.

options.t: Give the list — names, doses, the blood thinner — and the last two falls with dates. Ask for the falls service referral.
options.c: A referral to the falls clinic and a medication review. Two things that reduce the next fall.

options.t: 'They take a few tablets, I am not sure which.'
options.c: The list is the thing the nurse most needs and the thing you can most easily carry.

options.t: Give the blood thinner only.
options.c: Right drug; the interaction is in the rest.

steps.prompt: Home again. What changes?

options.t: The kitchen mat goes, a grab rail by the step, the falls-service appointment on the calendar, the medication list on the fridge, and a note of tonight's timeline.
options.c: Four small changes and a record. That is the carer's craft.

options.t: Nothing — it was a one-off.
options.c: Two falls in a season is a pattern, not a one-off.

options.t: Move them into your house.
options.c: Sometimes right. It is a decision for a calm week, with them.

complications.prompt: While waiting, they become confused about what day it is.

options.t: Tell the call handler now: new confusion after a head knock. It changes the urgency.
options.c: The ambulance is upgraded. New confusion was the sign.

options.t: Reassure them and wait.
options.c: Reassurance does not treat a bleed.

options.t: Ask them questions to test their memory.
options.c: You already know the answer. Say it to the handler.

complications.prompt: Your sibling texts: 'don't overreact, she always bumps her head'.

options.t: Reply with the fact — head knock on a blood thinner — and the advice line's answer; ask them to meet you at the hospital.
options.c: They arrive twenty minutes later and stop texting.

options.t: Follow their advice.
options.c: A text is not a clinician.

options.t: Ignore them.
options.c: You could. A fact and an invitation would have been better.

debrief: What two facts made this fall different, and where did you learn them?
How did you respect a refusal and still get the person seen?
Which of the five changes at home would you make first, and why?

transfer.check: Complete the carer self-identification: the role named, the local register or support service found, the first contact made.
transfer.note: The witnessed transfer check for this track is done live, on real material, with an assessor. This simulation rehearses judgement; it does not perform the check and it never credits the ledger.

scenarios.title: The boil-water notice at school
scenarios.role: Student or staff lead during a boil-water advisory
scenarios.site_default: a school on the local water system
scenarios.brief: A main break has put {site} under a boil-water advisory during the school day. The cafeteria serves lunch in an hour. Fountains are on. The message came by text to one office phone.
simulated: Serving food under an advisory
A fountain that stays on
A rumour that the water is 'poisoned'
live: Reading the advisory's exact wording
Taping off a fountain
Making the school's announcement script

steps.prompt: One office phone has the text. What first?

options.t: Confirm the advisory on the utility's own channel, then tell the principal and the cafeteria manager the exact wording — boil, not do-not-use — and start the fountain shut-off.
options.c: Confirmed. 'Boil' means ice, fountains and prep water; toilets and handwashing are fine. Now the plan fits the notice.

options.t: Announce over the tannoy that the water is unsafe.
options.c: 'Unsafe' is not what the notice says, and it starts the panic.

options.t: Tell the cafeteria to stop everything.
options.c: Lunch can be served on the advisory's terms. Read it first.

steps.prompt: Fountains: there are fourteen, some with bottle fillers.

options.t: Bag and tape every fountain and filler with a dated sign, and send bottled water or boiled-and-cooled water to each floor.
options.c: Fourteen fountains taped by two people in twenty minutes; water on every floor.

options.t: Tell students not to use them.
options.c: Telling is not taping. A fountain that runs will be used.

options.t: Turn off the mains to the building.
options.c: Toilets and handwashing stop with it. The advisory did not ask for that.

steps.prompt: The cafeteria manager asks: what can we serve?

options.t: From the notice: no ice from the machine, no drinks from the fountain, wash produce in bottled or boiled water, cook as normal, pre-packaged where possible. Write it and post it.
options.c: Lunch goes out on time, on the notice's terms.

options.t: Serve as normal — the heat kills everything.
options.c: Ice and washed salad never see heat.

options.t: Cancel lunch.
options.c: An option. The notice allowed a lunch; the children needed one.

steps.prompt: A parent posts that the water is 'poisoned' and children are 'being made to drink it'.

options.t: Reply on the school's channel with the utility's own wording and link, what the school did (fountains off, bottled water), and who to call.
options.c: The post gets corrected by other parents who read the source.

options.t: Ignore it.
options.c: A rumour with no answer becomes the story.

options.t: Say the water is fine.
options.c: It is not 'fine'; it is under a boil notice. Say what the notice says.

steps.prompt: The advisory lifts two days later. What happens before the fountains come back?

options.t: Flush every fountain and filler per the utility's lift instructions, log it, take the signs down last, and write the two days up for the next time.
options.c: Flushed, logged, signs down, a page in the file.

options.t: Take the tape off — it is lifted.
options.c: The pipes hold two days of standing water.

options.t: Leave the fountains taped for a week to be safe.
options.c: Cautious; the utility's flush instruction is the control.

complications.prompt: The science teacher wants to test the water 'to show the students'.

options.t: A field kit does not test for what a boil notice is about. Say so, and offer the utility's published test results as the lesson instead.
